1|# Window behavior
2|
3|## FF4A–FF4B — WY, WX: Window Y position, X position plus 7
4|
5|These two registers specify the on-screen coordinates of [the Window]'s top-left pixel.
6|
7|The Window is visible (if enabled) when `WX` and `WY` are in the range \[0; 166\] and \[0; 143\] respectively.
8|Values `WX`=7, `WY`=0 place the Window at the top left of the screen, completely covering the background.
9|
10|## Window mid-frame behavior
11|
12|While the Window should work as just mentioned, writing to `WX`, `WY` etc. mid-frame displays more articulated behavior.
13|There are several aspects of the window that respond differently to various mid-frame interactions; the **tl;dr** is this:
14|
15|- For the least glitchy results, only write to `WX`, `WY`, and `LCDC` during VBlank (possibly in your [VBlank interrupt handler]); if mid-frame writes are required, prefer writing during HBlank.
16|- If intending to hide the Window for part of the screen (e.g. to have a status bar at the *top* of the screen instead of the bottom), hide it by setting `WX` to a high value rather than writing to `LCDC`.
17|
18|### Window rendering criteria
19|
20|The PPU keeps track of a “**Y condition**” throughout a frame.
21|
22|- On each VBlank, the *Y condition* is cleared (becomes false).
23|- At the beginning of each scanline, if the value of `WY` is equal to [`LY`], the *Y condition* becomes true (and remains so for subsequent scanlines).
24|
25|:::tip Note
26|
27|On GBC, clearing the [Window enable bit] in `LCDC` resets the *Y condition*; `WY` must be set to `LY` or greater for the Window to display again in the current frame.
28|
29|:::
30|
31|Additionally, the PPU maintains a counter, initialized to 0 at the beginning of each scanline.
32|The counter is incremented for each pixel rendered; however, it also increments 7 times before the first pixel is actually rendered (this covers pixels discarded during the initial "fine scroll" adjustment).
33|
34|When this counter is equal to `WX`, if the *Y condition* is true and the [Window enable bit] is set in `LCDC`, background rendering is reset, beginning anew from the active row of the Window's tilemap.
35|The coordinate of the active Window row is then incremented.
36|
37|- This process can happen more than once per scanline, making the Window's "tilemap Y coordinate" increase more than once in the scanline.
38|  (This is demonstrated by the TODO test ROM.)
39|
40|  However, this requires "disabling" the Window by briefly clearing its enable bit from `LCDC` first.
41|- If this process doesn't happen, the Window's "tilemap Y coordinate" does not increase; so, if the Window is hidden (by any means) on a given scanline, the row of pixels rendered the next time it's shown will be the same as if it had not been hidden in the first place, producing a sort of vertical striped stretching:
42|
43|  ![Visual demonstration](https://github.com/mattcurrie/mealybug-tearoom-tests/raw/master/expected/DMG-blob/m2_win_en_toggle.png?raw=true)
44|- If `WX` is equal to 0, the Window is switched to before the initial "fine scroll" adjustment, causing it to be shifted left by <math><mi>SCX</mi> <mo>%</mo> <mn>8</mn></math> pixels.
45|- On monochrome systems, `WX` = 166 (which would normally show a single Window pixel, along the right edge of the screen) exhibits a bug: the Window spans the entire screen, but offset vertically by one scanline.
46|- On monochrome systems, if the Window is disabled via `LCDC`, but the other conditions are met *and* it would have started rendering exactly on a BG tile boundary, then where it would have started rendering, a single pixel with ID 0 (i.e. drawn as the first entry in [the BG palette]) is inserted; this offsets the remainder of the scanline.[^star_trek]
47|
48|[^star_trek]: This was discovered as affecting the game *Star Trek 25th anniversary*; more information and a test ROM are available [in this thread](https://github.com/LIJI32/SameBoy/issues/278#issuecomment-1189712129).
49|
50|[the Window]: #Window
51|[VBlank interrupt handler]: <#INT $40 — VBlank interrupt>
52|[Window enable bit]: <#LCDC.5 — Window enable>
53|[`LY`]: <#FF44 — LY: LCD Y coordinate \[read-only\]>
54|[the BG palette]: <#FF47 — BGP (Non-CGB Mode only): BG palette data>

; This test checks how the STAT register LY=LYC comparison bit and the
; corresponding interrupt behave when turning off and starting the PPU

; Verified results:
;   pass: DMG, MGB, SGB, SGB2, CGB, AGB, AGS
;   fail: -

.include "common.s"

  ld sp, DEFAULT_SP

  ld a, %01000000
  ldh (<STAT), a
  ld a, INTR_STAT
  ldh (<IE), a

; In this round we turn off the PPU while the comparison bit is true,
; and run tests where comparison bit changes
round1:
  ld hl, fail_intr_round1
  wait_vblank
  ld a, $90
  ldh (<LYC), a
  xor a
  ldh (<LCDC), a
  ldh (<IF), a
  ei
  nop

; The bit should be retained and not reset to 0
  ldh a, (<STAT)
  cp $c4
  jr z, +
  quit_failure_string "Fail: r1 step 1"

; Changing LYC should not have an effect, because the comparison
; clock is not running
+ ld a, $01
  ldh (<LYC), a
  ldh a, (<STAT)
  cp $c4
  jr z, +
  quit_failure_s

46|  ldh (<IF), a
47|  ei
48|  nop

52|  cp $c4
53|  jr z, +
54|  quit_failure_string "Fail: r1 step 1"
55|

57|; clock is not running
58|+ ld a, $01
59|  ldh (<LYC), a
60|  ldh a, (<STAT)
61|  cp $c4
62|  jr z, +
63|  quit_failure_string "Fail: r1 step 2"
64|

66|; The bit should go to 0, because LY=0
67|+ ld a, $80
68|  ldh (<LCDC), a
69|  ldh a, (<STAT)
70|  cp $c0
71|  jr z, round2
72|  quit_failure_string "Fail: r1 step 3"

75|; and run tests where comparison bit doesn't change
76|round2:
77|  di
78|  ld hl, fail_intr_round2
79|  wait_vblank
80|  ld a, $90
81|  ldh (<LYC), a
82|  xor a
83|  ldh (<LCDC), a
84|  ldh (<IF), a

86|  nop

106|; the comparison result doesn't change

108|  ldh (<LCDC), a

111|  jr z, round3

115|; and run tests where comparison bit doesn't change

120|  xor a
121|  ldh (<LYC), a
122|  ldh (<IF), a
123|  ldh (<LCDC), a
124|  ei
125|  nop
126|

128|  ldh a, (<STAT)
129|  cp $c0
130|  jr z, +
131|  quit_failure_string "Fail: r3 step 1"
132|

134|; we don't get a true bit from LY=00 comparison in the next step
135|+ ld a, $01
136|  ldh (<LYC), a
137|  ldh a, (<STAT)
138|  cp $c0
139|  jr z, +
140|  quit_failure_string "Fail: r3 step 2"
141|
142|; Enabling the PPU should have no effect, because we are now comparing
143|; LY=00 to LYC=01
144|+ ld a, $80
145|  ldh (<LCDC), a
146|  ldh a, (<STAT)
147|  cp $c0
148|  jr z, round4
149|  quit_failure_string "Fail: r3 step 3"
150|

152|; and run tests where comparison bit changes and we get an interrupt
153|round4:
154|  di
155|  wait_vblank
156|  xor a
157|  ldh (<LYC), a
158|  ldh (<IF), a
159|  ldh (<LCDC), a
160|  ei
161|  nop
162|
163|; The bit should not be set at this point
164|  ldh a, (<STAT)
165|  cp $c0
166|  jr z, +
167|  quit_failure_string "Fail: round 4"
168|

170|; clock starts running and the comparison bit gets set
171|+ ld a, $80
172|  ld hl, finish
173|  ldh (<LCDC), a
174|  di

182|fail_intr_round2:

1|# The Comprehensive Game Boy PPU Documentation
2|
3|These are my notes/findings based on the results of my test ROMs and subsequent implementation in my Game Boy emulator: [Beaten Dying Moon](https://mattcurrie.com/bdm-demo/)
4|
5|Familiarity with Kevin Horton's [Nitty Gritty Gameboy Cycle Timing](http://blog.kevtris.org/blogfiles/Nitty%20Gritty%20Gameboy%20VRAM%20Timing.txt) is assumed.  
6|
7|Any corrections or improvements are welcomed, especially for any already "known" information.
8|
9|## Registers
10|
11|### LCDC `$FF40`
12|
13|#### TILE_SEL (bit 4)
14|
15|The `TILE_SEL` bit of the `LCDC` register controls which area of VRAM is accessed when reading tile bitplane data.
16|
17|| TILE_SEL | VRAM Range               |
18|| -------- | ------------------------ |
19||        0 | $8800 - $97FF            |
20||        1 | $8000 - $8FFF (OBJ area) |
21|
22|The value of this bit can be written to at any time.
23|
24|`TILE_SEL` is read during the `0` and `1` stages of background tile data fetching. Changing its value during background tile data fetch allows for mixing tile bitplane data from two different tile patterns.
25|
26|On the CGB, there is strange behaviour if the value of this bit changes on particular T-cycles of the background tile data fetch. The following behaviour has been observed:
27|
28|- On all CGB revisions, setting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as a bitplane data read will cause it to use either:
29|  - bitplane 1 data from the most recently drawn sprite as bitplane data, if any, or
30|  - bitplane 1 data from the most recently drawn tile as when `TILE_SEL` was last reset, if any, or
31|  - bitplane 0 or 1 data from the read in progress during pixel 159/160 (?) on the previous row when the tile fetcher is interrupted. The timing of which bitplane is selected differs between CGB revisions.
32|- On all CGB revisions, excluding CPU CGB D, resetting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as a bitplane data read will cause the **tile index** to be instead used as the data for that bitplane.
33|- On CPU CGB D, resetting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as the bitplane 1 data read will cause the PPU to instead read the bitplane data from the address for bitplane 0.
34|
35|#### WIN_EN (bit 5)
36|
37|If WIN_EN is set then the window will be displayed when the WX and WY conditions are satisifed.
38|
39|Obscure behavior:
40|
41|- WIN_EN can be disabled during mode 3.  The disabling will take effect at the end of the current window tile being drawn. When the current window tile has finished being drawn, the PPU will start drawing background tiles again.
42|- When the background resumes drawing it is on a tile boundary. The low 3 bits of SCX have no effect. 
43|- Setting WIN_EN again during mode 3 on the same scanline will have no effect unless WX has been updated to set the window to activate on a pixel that hasn't been drawn yet.
44|- If WX has been updated correctly and WIN_EN is set again then the PPU stops drawing the background, and will activate the window again, but it will start drawing the **next row** of the window, on the same scanline.
45|
46|### SCY `$FF42`
47|
48|The `SCY` register controls the Y scroll of the background tile map.  
49|
50|The `SCY` register can be written to at any time. Writes will take effect immediately on the DMG. On CGB and AGB devices, writes appear to take effect 2 T-cycles later.
51|
52|On the DMG and CGB revisions up to and including the "CPU GBC C" revision, the `SCY` register is read during the background tile fetch `B`, `0` and `1` stages. Changing the value during background tile data fetch allows for mixing tile bitplane data from different rows of the tile.
53|
54|On the AGB and CGB revisions "CPU GBC D" and greater, the `SCY` register is only read during the `B` stage, so no tile bitplane data mixing can occur.
55|
56|

1|
2| Rendering overview 
3| Terminology 
4| The entire frame is not drawn atomically; instead, the image is drawn by the PPU (Pixel-Processing Unit) progressively, directly to the screen .
5|A frame consists of 154 scanlines ; during the first 144, the screen is drawn top to bottom, left to right. 
6| The main implication of this rendering process is the existence of raster effects : modifying some rendering parameters in the middle of rendering.
7|The most famous raster effect is modifying the scrolling registers between scanlines to create a “wavy” effect . 
8| A “ dot ” = one 2 22 Hz (≅ 4.194 MHz) time unit.
9|Dots remain the same regardless of whether the CPU is in Double Speed mode , so there are 4 dots per Normal Speed M-cycle, and 2 per Double Speed M-cycle. 
10|
11| NOTE 
12|
13| A frame is not exactly one 60 th of a second: the Game Boy runs slightly slower than 60 Hz, as one frame takes ~16.74 ms instead of ~16.67 (the error is 0.45%). 
14|
15| PPU modes 
16|
17| During a frame, the Game Boy’s PPU cycles between four modes as follows: 
18|
19| While the PPU is accessing some video-related memory, that memory is inaccessible to the CPU (writes are ignored, and reads return garbage values, usually $FF). 
20|
21| Mode Action Duration Accessible video memory 
22|
23| 2 Searching for OBJs which overlap this line 80 dots VRAM, CGB palettes 
24| 3 Sending pixels to the LCD Between 172 and 289 dots, see below None 
25| 0 Waiting until the end of the scanline 376 - mode 3’s duration VRAM, OAM, CGB palettes 
26| 1 Waiting until the next frame 4560 dots (10 scanlines) VRAM, OAM, CGB palettes 
27|
28| Mode 3 length 
29| During Mode 3, by default the PPU outputs one pixel to the screen per dot, from left to right; the screen is 160 pixels wide, so the minimum Mode 3 length is 160 + 12 1 = 172 dots. 
30| Unlike most game consoles, the Game Boy does not always output pixels steadily 2 : some features cause the rendering process to stall for a couple dots.
31|Any extra time spent stalling lengthens Mode 3; but since scanlines last for a fixed number of dots, Mode 0 is therefore shortened by that same amount of time. 
32| Three things can cause Mode 3 “penalties”: 
33|
34| Background scrolling : At the very beginning of Mode 3, rendering is paused for SCX % 8 dots while the same number of pixels are discarded from the leftmost tile. 
35| Window : After the last non-window pixel is emitted, a 6-dot penalty is incurred while the BG fetcher is being set up for the window. 
36| Objects : Each object drawn during the scanline (even partially) incurs a 6- to 11-dot penalty ( see below ). 
37|
38| On DMG and GBC in DMG mode, mid-scanline writes to BGP allow observing this behavior precisely, as any delay shifts the write’s effect to the left by that many dots. 
39| OBJ penalty algorithm 
40| Only the OBJ’s leftmost pixel matters here, transparent or not; it is designated as “The Pixel” in the following. 
41|
42| Determine the tile (background or window) that The Pixel is within. (This is affected by horizontal scrolling and/or the window!) 
43| If that tile has not been considered by a previous OBJ yet 3 :
44|
45| Count how many of that tile’s pixels are strictly to the right of The Pixel. 
46| Subtract 2. 
47| Incur this many dots of penalty, or zero if negative (from waiting for the BG fetch to finish). 
48|
49| Incur a flat, 6-dot penalty (from fetching the OBJ’s tile). 
50|
51| Exception : an OBJ with an OAM X position of 0 (thus, completely off the left side of the screen) always incurs a 11-dot penalty, regardless of SCX . 
52|

Read text file `/tmp/Rendering.html.txt`.
1|
2| Rendering overview 
3| Terminology 
4| The entire frame is not drawn atomically; instead, the image is drawn by the PPU (Pixel-Processing Unit) progressively, directly to the screen .
5|A frame consists of 154 scanlines ; during the first 144, the screen is drawn top to bottom, left to right. 
6| The main implication of this rendering process is the existence of raster effects : modifying some rendering parameters in the middle of rendering.
7|The most famous raster effect is modifying the scrolling registers between scanlines to create a “wavy” effect . 
8| A “ dot ” = one 2 22 Hz (≅ 4.194 MHz) time unit.
9|Dots remain the same regardless of whether the CPU is in Double Speed mode , so there are 4 dots per Normal Speed M-cycle, and 2 per Double Speed M-cycle. 
10|
11| NOTE 
12|
13| A frame is not exactly one 60 th of a second: the Game Boy runs slightly slower than 60 Hz, as one frame takes ~16.74 ms instead of ~16.67 (the error is 0.45%). 
14|
15| PPU modes 
16|
17| During a frame, the Game Boy’s PPU cycles between four modes as follows: 
18|
19| While the PPU is accessing some video-related memory, that memory is inaccessible to the CPU (writes are ignored, and reads return garbage values, usually $FF). 
20|
21| Mode Action Duration Accessible video memory 
22|
23| 2 Searching for OBJs which overlap this line 80 dots VRAM, CGB palettes 
24| 3 Sending pixels to the LCD Between 172 and 289 dots, see below None 
25| 0 Waiting until the end of the scanline 376 - mode 3’s duration VRAM, OAM, CGB palettes 
26| 1 Waiting until the next frame 4560 dots (10 scanlines) VRAM, OAM, CGB palettes 
27|
28| Mode 3 length 
29| During Mode 3, by default the PPU outputs one pixel to the screen per dot, from left to right; the screen is 160 pixels wide, so the minimum Mode 3 length is 160 + 12 1 = 172 dots. 
30| Unlike most game consoles, the Game Boy does not always output pixels steadily 2 : some features cause the rendering process to stall for a couple dots.
31|Any extra time spent stalling lengthens Mode 3; but since scanlines last for a fixed number of dots, Mode 0 is therefore shortened by that same amount of time. 
32| Three things can cause Mode 3 “penalties”: 
33|
34| Background scrolling : At the very beginning of Mode 3, rendering is paused for SCX % 8 dots while the same number of pixels are discarded from the leftmost tile. 
35| Window : After the last non-window pixel is emitted, a 6-dot penalty is incurred while the BG fetcher is being set up for the window. 
36| Objects : Each object drawn during the scanline (even partially) incurs a 6- to 11-dot penalty ( see below ). 
37|
38| On DMG and GBC in DMG mode, mid-scanline writes to BGP allow observing this behavior precisely, as any delay shifts the write’s effect to the left by that many dots. 
39| OBJ penalty algorithm 
40| Only the OBJ’s leftmost pixel matters here, transparent or not; it is designated as “The Pixel” in the following. 
41|
42| Determine the tile (background or window) that The Pixel is within. (This is affected by horizontal scrolling and/or the window!) 
43| If that tile has not been considered by a previous OBJ yet 3 :
44|
45| Count how many of that tile’s pixels are strictly to the right of The Pixel. 
46| Subtract 2. 
47| Incur this many dots of penalty, or zero if negative (from waiting for the BG fetch to finish). 
48|
49| Incur a flat, 6-dot penalty (from fetching the OBJ’s tile). 
50|
51| Exception : an OBJ with an OAM X position of 0 (thus, completely off the left side of the screen) always incurs a 11-dot penalty, regardless of SCX . 
52|
53| The 12 extra dots of penalty come from two tile fetches at the beginning of Mode 3. One is the first tile in the scanline (the one that gets shifted by SCX % 8 pixels), the other is simply discarded. ↩ 
54|
55| The Game Boy can afford to “take pauses”, because it writes to a LCD it fully controls; by contrast, home consoles like the NES or SNES are on a schedule imposed by the screen they are hooked up to. Taking pauses arguably simplified the PPU’s design while allowing greater flexibility to game developers. ↩ 
56|
57| Since pixels are emitted from left to right, OBJs overlapping the scanline are considered from leftmost to rightmost, with ties broken by their index / OAM address (lowest first). ↩ 
58|
59|

Read text file `/tmp/STAT.html.txt`.
1|
2| LCD Status Registers 
3|
4| TERMINOLOGY 
5|
6| A dot is the shortest period over which the PPU can output one pixel: is it equivalent to 1 T-cycle on DMG or on CGB Normal Speed mode or 2 T-cycles on CGB Double Speed mode. On each dot during mode 3, either the PPU outputs a pixel or the fetcher is stalling the FIFOs . 
7|
8| FF44 — LY: LCD Y coordinate [read-only] 
9| LY indicates the current horizontal line, which might be about to be drawn,
10|being drawn, or just been drawn. LY can hold any value from 0 to 153, with
11|values from 144 to 153 indicating the VBlank period. 
12| FF45 — LYC: LY compare 
13| The Game Boy constantly compares the value of the LYC and LY registers.
14|When both values are identical, the “LYC=LY” flag in the STAT register
15|is set, and (if enabled) a STAT interrupt is requested. 
16| FF41 — STAT: LCD status 
17|
18| 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 
19|
20| LYC int select Mode 2 int select Mode 1 int select Mode 0 int select LYC == LY PPU mode 
21|
22| LYC int select ( Read/Write ): If set, selects the LYC == LY condition for the STAT interrupt . 
23| Mode 2 int select ( Read/Write ): If set, selects the Mode 2 condition for the STAT interrupt . 
24| Mode 1 int select ( Read/Write ): If set, selects the Mode 1 condition for the STAT interrupt . 
25| Mode 0 int select ( Read/Write ): If set, selects the Mode 0 condition for the STAT interrupt . 
26| LYC == LY ( Read-only ): Set when LY contains the same value as LYC ; it is constantly updated. 
27| PPU mode ( Read-only ): Indicates the PPU’s current status . Reports 0 instead when the PPU is disabled . 
28|
29| Spurious STAT interrupts 
30| A hardware quirk in the monochrome Game Boy makes the LCD interrupt
31|sometimes trigger when writing to STAT (including writing $00) during
32|OAM scan, HBlank, VBlank, or LY=LYC. It behaves as if $FF were
33|written for one M-cycle, and then the written value were written the next
34|M-cycle. Because the GBC in DMG mode does not have this quirk, two games
35|that depend on this quirk (Ocean’s Road Rash and Vic Tokai’s Xerd
36|no Densetsu ) will not run on a GBC. 
37|
38|

Status: 6/12 passing on `mooneye:ppu` (was 3/12), no regressions.

What changed this turn (all under `core/`):
- `core/ppu.ts`, `core/index.ts`: OAM reads return `$FF` and VRAM reads return `$FF` while the PPU blocks them; CPU writes to OAM/VRAM ignored while blocked. This fixed `intr_2_oam_ok_timing`.
- `core/ppu.ts`: STAT coincidence bit now visible on reads (`0xf8`→`0xfc` mask bug); LCD-off retains the coincidence latch and freezes the STAT line; LCD-on recomputes coincidence with edge detection and starts line 0 in mode 0 (no OAM search). This fixed `stat_lyc_onoff` and `stat_irq_blocking`.
- `core/ppu.ts`: mode-3 sprite penalty replaced with the Pan Docs OBJ-penalty algorithm (per-sprite 6 dots + first-per-tile BG-wait, X=0 handling). Just fixed an X=0 overcount (repeat X=0 sprites in one tile cost 6, not 11) — rescore still pending.
- `core/index.ts`: snapshot/restore extended for the new `line0` flag.

Still failing: `hblank_ly_scx_timing`, `intr_2_0_timing`, `sprites`, `lcdon_timing`, `lcdon_write_timing`, `vblank_stat_intr`. Analysis and test sources are in hand; next steps are rescoring the X=0 fix, then probe-driven calibration of the line-0 length, STAT pipeline lag, mode-2-at-144 quirk, and interrupt/halt phase.

payload.prompt:
# Repair task

Edit files under core/ only. The gate reads only the diff of core/** and refuses a diff that touches any other
path, adds a literal over the gate's literal limit, or contains the incident's frame hash or trace bytes.
Your budget is 90 model steps and 1350 s of wall clock, after which you are stopped and an empty diff is refused, so make your first edit under core/ by step 45 (675 s) and refine it with the replay after.

## Core API (core/index.ts)
export function createCore(rom: Uint8Array): Core;  // step, runFrame, runToCounter(n), cpu, read, frame() (160*144 shades 0..3),
                                                    // serial, cycles, setButtons(mask), snapshot/restore, tap
export const HANDLERS: Record<HandlerId, string>;  // handler id -> implementing file under core/

## The task
packet/task.json names the task. For an incident: packet/incident.json (first diverging counter, signature),
packet/trace.json (inputs and the window n-60 .. n+120), and the evidence files (core.png, oracle.png, diff.png,
regwrites.jsonl, window.json) under packet/evidence/. packet/roms.json lists the ROMs per family.

## Replay
node tools/replay.mjs --incident <INC-id> --core-dir core --evidence-dir packet/evidence
    reruns the window n-60..n+120 on core/ against the cached oracle frames; prints the first mismatch or "clean"
node tools/replay.mjs --family <family> --core-dir core --roms packet/roms.json
    scores one family; prints its reading as JSON
ROMs and oracle frames are reached through $RATCHET_ROMS and $RATCHET_CACHE.

## Skills
.agents/skills/ holds the skills shown to this attempt, read-only. Mark each one in RESULT.json.

## End by writing packet/RESULT.json
{ "dispositions": { "<SKL-id>": "applied" | "considered-not-applicable" },
  "off_map": null | "<one sentence naming a lesson you relied on that no shown skill holds>",
  "beliefs": [ { "claim": "<a hardware claim>", "false_if": "<the observation that falsifies it>" } ],
  "summary": "<one sentence: what the diff changes>" }

payload.prompt:
# Repair task

Edit files under core/ only. The gate reads only the diff of core/** and refuses a diff that touches any other
path, adds a literal over the gate's literal limit, or contains the incident's frame hash or trace bytes.
Your budget is 90 model steps and 1350 s of wall clock, after which you are stopped and an empty diff is refused, so make your first edit under core/ by step 45 (675 s) and refine it with the replay after.

## Core API (core/index.ts)
export function createCore(rom: Uint8Array): Core;  // step, runFrame, runToCounter(n), cpu, read, frame() (160*144 shades 0..3),
                                                    // serial, cycles, setButtons(mask), snapshot/restore, tap
export const HANDLERS: Record<HandlerId, string>;  // handler id -> implementing file under core/

## The task
packet/task.json names the task. For an incident: packet/incident.json (first diverging counter, signature),
packet/trace.json (inputs and the window n-60 .. n+120), and the evidence files (core.png, oracle.png, diff.png,
regwrites.jsonl, window.json) under packet/evidence/. packet/roms.json lists the ROMs per family.

## Replay
node tools/replay.mjs --incident <INC-id> --core-dir core --evidence-dir packet/evidence
    reruns the window n-60..n+120 on core/ against the cached oracle frames; prints the first mismatch or "clean"
node tools/replay.mjs --family <family> --core-dir core --roms packet/roms.json
    scores one family; prints its reading as JSON
ROMs and oracle frames are reached through $RATCHET_ROMS and $RATCHET_CACHE.

## Skills
.agents/skills/ holds the skills shown to this attempt, read-only. Mark each one in RESULT.json.

## End by writing packet/RESULT.json
{ "dispositions": { "<SKL-id>": "applied" | "considered-not-applicable" },
  "off_map": null | "<one sentence naming a lesson you relied on that no shown skill holds>",
  "beliefs": [ { "claim": "<a hardware claim>", "false_if": "<the observation that falsifies it>" } ],
  "summary": "<one sentence: what the diff changes>" }

## Policy lines
- Run node tools/replay.mjs on the task before the first edit and after each edit; write RESULT.json only once it prints clean.

21|; Turns bit 5 (WIN_EN) of LCDC register on and off multiple times 
22|; during mode 3. 
23|; If WX is set to activate at a pixel that has not been drawn yet, and WIN_EN
24|; is toggled then the window can be turned on and off multiple times on a single
25|; row, with background tiles displaying in between.
26|; The current row of the window is incremented each time the window is activated,
27|; so the second time the window is activated on the row, the next row of window
28|; pixels are displayed.
29|; When the window is disabled during mode 3, the tile fetcher will read from the
30|; background tiles instead of the window tiles at the start of the next tile 
31|; fetcher cycle.  This means that when the window is turned on and off it will
32|; always display a multiple of 8 pixels, except when the window begins off the
33|; left edge of the screen.

  "output": "# The Comprehensive Game Boy PPU Documentation

These are my notes/findings based on the results of my test ROMs and subsequent implementation in my Game Boy emulator: [Beaten Dying Moon](https://mattcurrie.com/bdm-demo/)

Familiarity with Kevin Horton's [Nitty Gritty Gameboy Cycle Timing](http://blog.kevtris.org/blogfiles/Nitty%20Gritty%20Gameboy%20VRAM%20Timing.txt) is assumed.  

Any corrections or improvements are welcomed, especially for any already "known" information.

## Registers

### LCDC `$FF40`

#### TILE_SEL (bit 4)

The `TILE_SEL` bit of the `LCDC` register controls which area of VRAM is accessed when reading tile bitplane data.

| TILE_SEL | VRAM Range               |
| -------- | ------------------------ |
|        0 | $8800 - $97FF            |
|        1 | $8000 - $8FFF (OBJ area) |

The value of this bit can be written to at any time.

`TILE_SEL` is read during the `0` and `1` stages of background tile data fetching. Changing its value during background tile data fetch allows for mixing tile bitplane data from two different tile patterns.

On the CGB, there is strange behaviour if the value of this bit changes on particular T-cycles of the background tile data fetch. The following behaviour has been observed:

- On all CGB revisions, setting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as a bitplane data read will cause it to use either:
  - bitplane 1 data from the most recently drawn sprite as bitplane data, if any, or
  - bitplane 1 data from the most recently drawn tile as when `TILE_SEL` was last reset, if any, or
  - bitplane 0 or 1 data from the read in progress during pixel 159/160 (?) on the previous row when the tile fetcher is interrupted. The timing of which bitplane is selected differs between CGB revisions.
- On all CGB revisions, excluding CPU CGB D, resetting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as a bitplane data read will cause the **tile index** to be instead used as the data for that bitplane.
- On CPU CGB D, resetting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as the bitplane 1 data read will cause the PPU to instead read the bitplane data from the address for bitplane 0.

#### WIN_EN (bit 5)

If WIN_EN is set then the window will be displayed when the WX and WY conditions are satisifed.

Obscure behavior:

- WIN_EN can be disabled during mode 3.  The disabling will take effect at the end of the current window tile being drawn. When the current window tile has finished being drawn, the PPU will start drawing background tiles again.
- When the background resumes drawing it is on a tile boundary. The low 3 bits of SCX have no effect. 
- Setting WIN_EN again during mode 3 on the same scanline will have no effect unless WX has been updated to set the window to activate on a pixel that hasn't been drawn yet.
- If WX has been updated correctly and WIN_EN is set again then the PPU stops drawing the background, and will activate the window again, but it will start drawing the **next row** of the window, on the same scanline.

### SCY `$FF42`

The `SCY` register controls the Y scroll of the background tile map.  

The `SCY` register can be written to at any time. Writes will take effect immediately on the DMG. On CGB and AGB devices, writes appear to take effect 2 T-cycles later.

On the DMG and CGB revisions up to and including the "CPU GBC C" revision, the `SCY` register is read during the background tile fetch `B`, `0` and `1` stages. Changing the value during background tile data fetch allows for mixing tile bitplane data from different rows of the tile.

On the AGB and CGB revisions "CPU GBC D" and greater, the `SCY` register is only read during the `B` stage, so no tile bitplane data mixing can occur.

import struct, zlib
def read_png(path):
    d = open(path,'rb').read()
    assert d[:8] == b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n'
    pos = 8; w=h=None; bitd=None; coltype=None; idat=b''
    while pos < len(d):
        ln = struct.unpack('>I', d[pos:pos+4])[0]
        typ = d[pos+4:pos+8]
        data = d[pos+8:pos+8+ln]
        if typ == b'IHDR':
            w,h,bitd,coltype,comp,filt,inter = struct.unpack('>IIBBBBB', data)
        elif typ == b'IDAT':
            idat += data
        pos += 12 + ln
    raw = zlib.decompress(idat)
    ch = {0:1,2:3,4:2,6:4}[coltype]
    # assume bitd 8 for coltype>=2 else grayscale 1/2/4/8
    import math
    if coltype == 0:
        stride = math.ceil(w*bitd/8)
    else:
        stride = w*ch*bitd//8
    px = [[0]*w for _ in range(h)]
    prev = bytearray(stride)
    p = 0
    for y in range(h):
        f = raw[p]; p+=1
        line = bytearray(raw[p:p+stride]); p+=stride
        if f==1:
            for i in range(ch,stride): line[i]=(line[i]+line[i-ch])&0xff
        elif f==2:
            for i in range(stride): line[i]=(line[i]+prev[i])&0xff
        elif f==3:
            for i in range(stride):
                a=line[i-ch] if i>=ch else 0
                line[i]=(line[i]+((a+prev[i])>>1))&0xff
        elif f==4:
            for i in range(stride):
                a=line[i-ch] if i>=ch else 0
                b=prev[i]
                c=prev[i-ch] if i>=ch else 0
                q=a+b-c
                pa=abs(q-a);pb=abs(q-b);pc=abs(q-c)
                pr=a if (pa<=pb and pa<=pc) else (b if pb<=pc else c)
                line[i]=(line[i]+pr)&0xff
        prev=line
        if coltype==0 and bitd<8:
            per=8//bitd; mask=(1<<bitd)-1
            for x in range(w):

            for x in range(w): px[y][x]=line[x]
        else:
            for x in range(w):
                r=line[x*ch]

21|; Tests the values of LY, STAT, and read accessibility of OAM and VRAM after
22|; the PPU is enabled by writing to LCDC.
23|; Expectations
24|;   - line 0 starts with mode 0 and goes straight to mode 3
25|;   - line 0 has different timings because the PPU is late by 2 T-cycles
26|;   - line 1 and line 2 have normal timings
27|
28|; Verified results:
29|;   pass: DMG, MGB, SGB, SGB2
30|;   fail: CGB, AGB, AGS
31|
32|; On real hardware, failures can be grouped into two categories:
33|;   CGB before D: failure
34|;   CGB D, E, AGB, AGS: different failure than pre-D CGBs
35|
36|.include "common.s"
37|
38|  ld sp, DEFAULT_SP
39|
40|  call disable_ppu_safe
41|  call clear_vram
42|  call clear_oam
43|
44|test_ly:
45|  ld de, LY
46|  call test_passes
47|  ld de, expect_ly
48|  call verify_results
49|
50|test_stat_lyc0:
51|  xor a
52|  ldh (<LYC), a
53|  ld de, STAT
54|  call test_passes
55|  ld de, expect_stat_lyc0
56|  call verify_results
57|
58|test_stat_lyc1:
59|  ld a, $01
60|  ldh (<LYC), a
61|  ld de, STAT
62|  call test_passes
63|  ld de, expect_stat_lyc1
64|  call verify_results
65|
66|test_oam_access:
67|  ld de, OAM
68|  call test_passes
69|  ld de, expect_oam_access
70|  call verify_results
71|
72|test_vram_access:
73|  ld de, VRAM
74|  call test_passes
75|  ld de, expect_vram_access
76|  call verify_results
77|
78|test_finish:
79|  quit_ok
80|
81|.bank 1 slot 1
82|.section "Test_expectations" FREE
83|
84|; Each read in a test pass can be seen as equivalent to this:
85|;   ldh (<LCDC), a
86|;   nops XXX   <- cycle count goes here
87|;   ld a, (de)
88|cycle_counts:
89|.db 0   17  60  110 130 174 224 244
90|.db 1   18  61  111 131 175 225 245
91|.db 2   19  62  112 132 176 226 246
92|
93|expect_ly:
94|.db $00 $00 $00 $00 $01 $01 $01 $02
95|.db $00 $00 $00 $01 $01 $01 $02 $02
96|.db $00 $00 $00 $01 $01 $01 $02 $02
97|.db "LY" $00
98|
99|expect_stat_lyc0:
100|.db $84 $84 $87 $84 $82 $83 $80 $82
101|.db $84 $87 $84 $80 $82 $80 $80 $82
102|.db $84 $87 $84 $82 $83 $80 $82 $83
103|.db "STAT LYC=0" $00
104|
105|expect_stat_lyc1:
106|.db $80 $80 $83 $80 $86 $87 $84 $82
107|.db $80 $83 $80 $80 $86 $84 $80 $82
108|.db $80 $83 $80 $86 $87 $84 $82 $83
109|.db "STAT LYC=1" $00
110|
111|expect_oam_access:
112|.db $00 $00 $FF $00 $FF $FF $00 $FF
113|.db $00 $FF $00 $FF $FF $00 $FF $FF
114|.db $00 $FF $00 $FF $FF $00 $FF $FF
115|.db "OAM access" $00
116|
117|expect_vram_access:
118|.db $00 $00 $FF $00 $00 $FF $00 $00
119|.db $00 $FF $00 $00 $FF $00 $00 $FF
120|.db $00 $FF $00 $00 $FF $00 $00 $FF
121|.db "VRAM access" $00
122|
123|; Inputs:
124|;   DE: test expectations pointer
125|verify_results:
126|  push de
127|
128|  ld c, $00
129|  ld hl, hram.pass1_results
130|
131|- ld a, (hl)
132|  ld b, a
133|  ld a, (de)
134|  cp b
135|  jp nz, verify_fail
136|  inc de
137|  inc hl
138|  inc c
139|  ld a, c
140|  cp 24
141|  jr nz, -
142|
143|  pop de
144|  ret
145|
146|verify_fail:
147|  ld a, (hl)
148|  ld (hram.fail_actual), a
149|  ld a, (de)
150|  ld (hram.fail_expect), a
151|  ld a, c
152|  ld (hram.fail_round), a
153|  pop de
154|  ld h, $00
155|  ld l, 24
156|  add hl, de
157|  ld a, l
158|  ld (hram.fail_str_l), a
159|  ld a, h
160|  ld (hram.fail_str_h), a
161|
162|  quit_inline
163|  print_string_literal "Test failed: "
164|  call print_newline
165|  ld a, (hram.fail_str_l)
166|  ld c, a
167|  ld a, (hram.fail_str_h)
168|  ld b, a
169|  call print_string
170|  call print_newline
171|  call print_newline
172|
173|  print_string_literal "Cycle:    $"
174|  push hl
175|  ld hl, cycle_counts
176|  ld b, $00
177|  ld a, (hram.fail_round)
178|  ld c, a
179|  add hl, bc
180|  ld a, (hl)
181|  pop hl
182|  call print_hex8
183|  call print_newline
184|
185|  print_string_literal "Expected: $"
186|  ld a, (hram.fail_expect)
187|  call print_hex8
188|  call print_newline
189|
190|  print_string_literal "Actual:   $"
191|  ld a, (hram.fail_actual)
192|  call print_hex8
193|
194|  ld d, $42
195|  ret
196|
197|.ends
198|
199|.ramsection "Test-State" slot HRAM_SLOT
200|  hram.pass1_results dsb 8
201|  hram.pass2_results dsb 8
202|  hram.pass3_results dsb 8
203|  hram.fail_round db
204|  hram.fail_expect db
205|  hram.fail_actual db
206|  hram.fail_str .dw
207|  hram.fail_str_l db
208|  hram.fail_str_h db
209|.ends
210|
211|.bank 1 slot 1
212|.section "Test_passes" FREE
213|
214|; Inputs:
215|;   DE address to read
216|; Preserved: -
217|test_passes:
218|
219|.macro test_reads
220|  ld a, (de)  ; 0
221|  ld (hl+), a
222|  nops 13
223|  ld a, (de)  ; 17
224|  ld (hl+), a
225|  nops 39
226|  ld a, (de)  ; 60
227|  ld (hl+), a
228|  nops 46
229|  ld a, (de)  ; 110
230|  ld (hl+), a
231|  nops 16
232|  ld a, (de)  ; 130
233|  ld (hl+), a
234|  nops 40
235|  ld a, (de)  ; 174
236|  ld (hl+), a
237|  nops 46
238|  ld a, (de)  ; 224
239|  ld (hl+), a
240|  nops 16
241|  ld a, (de)  ; 244
242|  ld (hl+), a
243|.endm
244|
245|test_pass1:
246|  ld hl, hram.pass1_results
247|  ld a, $81
248|  ldh (<LCDC), a
249|  test_reads
250|  call disable_ppu_safe
251|
252|test_pass2:
253|  ld hl, hram.pass2_results
254|  ld a, $81
255|  ldh (<LCDC), a
256|  nops 1
257|  test_reads
258|  call disable_ppu_safe
259|
260|test_pass3:
261|  ld hl, hram.pass3_results
262|  ld a, $81
263|  ldh (<LCDC), a
264|  nops 2
265|  test_reads
266|  jp disable_ppu_safe
267|
268|.ends

20|
21|; Tests how SCX affects the duration between STAT mode=0 interrupt and LY increment.
22|; No sprites or window.
23|;
24|; Expected behaviour:
25|;   (SCX mod 8) = 0   => LY increments 51 cycles after STAT interrupt
26|;   (SCX mod 8) = 1-4 => LY increments 50 cycles after STAT interrupt
27|;   (SCX mod 8) = 5-7 => LY increments 49 cycles after STAT interrupt
28|
29|; Verified results:
30|;   pass: DMG, MGB, SGB, SGB2
31|;   fail: CGB, AGB, AGS
32|
33|.include "common.s"
34|
35|.macro clear_interrupts
36|  xor a
37|  ldh (<IF), a
38|.endm
39|
40|.macro scroll_x ARGS value
41|  ld a, value
42|  ldh (<SCX), a
43|.endm
44|
45|  ld sp, DEFAULT_SP
46|
47|  wait_vblank
48|  ld hl, LY
49|  ld a, $08
50|  ldh (<STAT), a
51|  ld a, INTR_STAT
52|  ldh (<IE), a
53|
54|.macro perform_test ARGS scanline delay_a delay_b
55|  ld d, scanline - 1
56|  ld e, scanline
57|  test_iter scanline delay_a
58|  cp d
59|  jp nz, test_fail
60|  test_iter scanline delay_b
61|  cp e
62|  jp nz, test_fail
63|.endm
64|
65|.macro test_iter ARGS scanline delay
66|  call setup_and_wait
67|  ; Interrupt processing: 5
68|  ; Interrupt vector: 4 + 4 = 8
69|  call standard_delay
70|  ; 6 + 23 + 4
71|  nops delay
72|  ; N cycles
73|  ld a, (hl)
74|  ; 1 cycle for decoding before memory read
75|  ; 5 + 4 + 4 + 6 + 23 + 4 + N + 1
76|  ; = 47 + N cycles before memory read
77|.endm
78|
79|  perform_test $42 2 3
80|  perform_test $43 2 3
81|  scroll_x $01
82|  perform_test $42 1 2
83|  perform_test $43 1 2
84|  scroll_x $02
85|  perform_test $42 1 2
86|  perform_test $43 1 2
87|  scroll_x $03
88|  perform_test $42 1 2
89|  perform_test $43 1 2
90|  scroll_x $04
91|  perform_test $42 1 2
92|  perform_test $43 1 2
93|  scroll_x $05
94|  perform_test $42 0 1
95|  perform_test $43 0 1
96|  scroll_x $06
97|  perform_test $42 0 1
98|  perform_test $43 0 1
99|  scroll_x $07
100|  perform_test $42 0 1
101|  perform_test $43 0 1
102|  scroll_x $08
103|  perform_test $42 2 3
104|  perform_test $43 2 3
105|
106|  quit_ok
107|
108|test_fail:
109|  ld b, a
110|  ldh a, (<SCX)
111|  setup_assertions
112|  ; A = SCX
113|  ; B = LY value
114|  ; D = scanline - 1
115|  ; E = scanline
116|  quit_failure_dump
117|
118|standard_delay:
119|  nops 23
120|  ret
121|
122|setup_and_wait:
123|  wait_vblank
124|- ldh a, (<LY)
125|  cp d
126|  jr nz, -
127|  clear_interrupts
128|  ei
129|
130|  halt
131|  nop
132|  jp fail_halt
133|
134|fail_halt:
135|  quit_failure_string "FAIL: HALT"
136|
137|.org INTR_VEC_STAT
138|  add sp,+2
139|  ret

 Mode 3 length 
 During Mode 3, by default the PPU outputs one pixel to the screen per dot, from left to right; the screen is 160 pixels wide, so the minimum Mode 3 length is 160 + 12 1 = 172 dots. 
 Unlike most game consoles, the Game Boy does not always output pixels steadily 2 : some features cause the rendering process to stall for a couple dots.
Any extra time spent stalling lengthens Mode 3; but since scanlines last for a fixed number of dots, Mode 0 is therefore shortened by that same amount of time. 
 Three things can cause Mode 3 “penalties”: 
 
 Background scrolling : At the very beginning of Mode 3, rendering is paused for SCX % 8 dots while the same number of pixels are discarded from the leftmost tile. 
 Window : After the last non-window pixel is emitted, a 6-dot penalty is incurred while the BG fetcher is being set up for the window. 
 Objects : Each object drawn during the scanline (even partially) incurs a 6- to 11-dot penalty ( see below ). 
 
 On DMG and GBC in DMG mode, mid-scanline writes to BGP allow observing this behavior precisely, as any delay shifts the write’s effect to the left by that many dots. 
 OBJ penalty algorithm 
 Only the OBJ’s leftmost pixel matters here, transparent or not; it is designated as “The Pixel” in the following. 
 
 Determine the tile (background or window) that The Pixel is within. (This is affected by horizontal scrolling and/or the window!) 
 If that tile has not been considered by a previous OBJ yet 3 :
 
 Count how many of that tile’s pixels are strictly to the right of The Pixel. 
 Subtract 2. 
 Incur this many dots of penalty, or zero if negative (from waiting for the BG fetch to finish). 
 
 
 Incur a flat, 6-dot penalty (from fetching the OBJ’s tile). 
 
 Exception : an OBJ with an OAM X position of 0 (thus, completely off the left side of the screen) always incurs a 11-dot penalty, regardless of SCX . 
 
 
 
 The 12 extra dots of penalty come from two tile fetches at the beginning of Mode 3. One is the first tile in the scanline (the one that gets shifted by SCX % 8 pixels), the other is simply discarded. ↩ 
 
 
 The Game Boy can afford to “take pauses”, because it writes to a LCD it fully controls; by contrast, home consoles like the NES or SNES are on a schedule imposed by the screen they are hooked up to. Taking pauses arguably simplified the PPU’s design while allowing greater flexibility to game developers. ↩ 
 
 
 Since pixels are emitted from left to right, OBJs overlapping the scanline are considered from leftmost to rightmost, with ties broken by their index / OAM address (lowest first). ↩

21|; Tests whether writes to OAM and VRAM pass after the PPU is enabled by
22|; writing to LCDC.
23|
24|; Verified results:
25|;   pass: DMG, MGB, SGB, SGB2
26|;   fail: CGB, AGB, AGS
27|
28|.include "common.s"
29|
30|  ld sp, DEFAULT_SP
31|
32|  call disable_ppu_safe
33|  call clear_vram
34|  call clear_oam
35|
36|test_oam_access:
37|  ld de, OAM
38|  call run_tests
39|  ld de, expect_oam_access
40|  call verify_results
41|
42|test_vram_access:
43|  ld de, VRAM
44|  call run_tests
45|  ld de, expect_vram_access
46|  call verify_results
47|
48|test_finish:
49|  quit_ok
50|
51|.bank 1 slot 1
52|.section "Test_expectations" FREE
53|
54|; Each write in a test pass can be seen as equivalent to this:
55|;   ldh (<LCDC), a <- PPU enabled
56|;   nops XXX       <- nop count goes here
57|;   ld (de), a
58|nop_counts:
59|.db 0   17  18  60  61  110 111
60|.db 112 130 131 132 174 175 224 225
61|.db 226 244 245 246
62|
63|expect_oam_access:
64|.db $81 $81 $00 $00 $81 $81 $81
65|.db $00 $00 $81 $00 $00 $81 $81 $81
66|.db $00 $00 $81 $00
67|.db "OAM write" $00
68|
69|expect_vram_access:
70|.db $81 $81 $00 $00 $81 $81 $81
71|.db $81 $81 $81 $00 $00 $81 $81 $81
72|.db $81 $81 $81 $00
73|.db "VRAM write" $00
74|
75|; Inputs:
76|;   DE: test expectations pointer
77|verify_results:
78|  push de
79|
80|  ld c, $00
81|  ld hl, wram.test_results
82|
83|- ld a, (hl)
84|  ld b, a
85|  ld a, (de)
86|  cp b
87|  jp nz, verify_fail
88|  inc de
89|  inc hl
90|  inc c
91|  ld a, c
92|  cp 19
93|  jr nz, -
94|
95|  pop de
96|  ret
97|
98|verify_fail:
99|  ld a, (hl)
100|  ld (hram.fail_actual), a
101|  ld a, (de)
102|  ld (hram.fail_expect), a
103|  ld a, c
104|  ld (hram.fail_round), a
105|  pop de
106|  ld h, $00
107|  ld l, 19
108|  add hl, de
109|  ld a, l
110|  ld (hram.fail_str_l), a
111|  ld a, h
112|  ld (hram.fail_str_h), a
113|
114|  quit_inline
115|  print_string_literal "Test failed: "
116|  call print_newline
117|  ld a, (hram.fail_str_l)
118|  ld c, a
119|  ld a, (hram.fail_str_h)
120|  ld b, a
121|  call print_string
122|  call print_newline
123|  call print_newline
124|
125|  print_string_literal "Cycle:    $"
126|  push hl
127|  ld hl, nop_counts
128|  ld b, $00
129|  ld a, (hram.fail_round)
130|  ld c, a
131|  add hl, bc
132|  ld a, (hl)
133|  pop hl
134|  call print_hex8
135|  call print_newline
136|
137|  print_string_literal "Expected: $"
138|  ld a, (hram.fail_expect)
139|  call print_hex8
140|  call print_newline
141|
142|  print_string_literal "Actual:   $"
143|  ld a, (hram.fail_actual)
144|  call print_hex8
145|
146|  ld d, $42
147|  ret
148|
149|.ends
150|
151|.ramsection "Test-WRAM" slot WRAM0_SLOT
152|  wram.test_code dsb 300
153|  wram.test_results dsb 19
154|.ends
155|
156|.ramsection "Test-HRAM" slot HRAM_SLOT
157|  hram.fail_round db
158|  hram.fail_expect db
159|  hram.fail_actual db
160|  hram.fail_str .dw
161|  hram.fail_str_l db
162|  hram.fail_str_h db
163|.ends
164|
165|.bank 1 slot 1
166|.section "Test_case" FREE
167|
168|; Inputs:
169|;   DE address to read
170|; Preserved: -
171|run_tests:
172|  ld hl, nop_counts
173|  ld bc, wram.test_results
174|  xor a
175|
176|- cp 19
177|  ret z
178|
179|  push af
180|  ld a, (hl+)
181|  push hl
182|  ld h, b
183|  ld l, c
184|
185|  call test_case
186|
187|  ld b, h
188|  ld c, l
189|  pop hl
190|  pop af
191|  inc a
192|
193|  jr -
194|
195|; Inputs:
196|;   A number of nops
197|;   DE address to read
198|;   HL test result pointer
199|; Outputs:
200|;   DE address to read
201|;   HL test result pointer + 1
202|test_case:
203|  push hl
204|  push de
205|  push af
206|  xor a
207|  ld (OAM), a
208|  ld (VRAM), a
209|
210|  ; Copy test case prologue code
211|  ld hl, wram.test_code
212|  ld de, test_case_prologue
213|  ld bc, test_case_epilogue - test_case_prologue
214|  call memcpy
215|
216|  ; Add nops
217|  pop af
218|- and a
219|  jr z, +
220|  dec a
221|  ld (hl), $00
222|  inc hl
223|  jr -
224|+
225|
226|  ; Copy test case epilogue code
227|  ld de, test_case_epilogue
228|  ld bc, test_case_end - test_case_epilogue
229|  call memcpy
230|
231|  pop de
232|  call wram.test_code
233|  call disable_ppu_safe
234|
235|  pop hl
236|  ld a, (de)
237|  ld (hl+), a
238|  ret
239|
240|test_case_prologue:
241|  ld a, $81
242|  ldh (<LCDC), a
243|  ; nops will be added here
244|test_case_epilogue:
245|  ld (de), a
246|  ret
247|test_case_end:
248|
249|.ends

payload.prompt:
# Repair task

Edit files under core/ only. The gate reads only the diff of core/** and refuses a diff that touches any other
path, adds a literal over the gate's literal limit, or contains the incident's frame hash or trace bytes.
Your budget is 90 model steps and 1350 s of wall clock, after which you are stopped and an empty diff is refused, so make your first edit under core/ by step 45 (675 s) and refine it with the replay after.

## Core API (core/index.ts)
export function createCore(rom: Uint8Array): Core;  // step, runFrame, runToCounter(n), cpu, read, frame() (160*144 shades 0..3),
                                                    // serial, cycles, setButtons(mask), snapshot/restore, tap
export const HANDLERS: Record<HandlerId, string>;  // handler id -> implementing file under core/

## The task
packet/task.json names the task. For an incident: packet/incident.json (first diverging counter, signature),
packet/trace.json (inputs and the window n-60 .. n+120), and the evidence files (core.png, oracle.png, diff.png,
regwrites.jsonl, window.json) under packet/evidence/. packet/roms.json lists the ROMs per family.

## Replay
node tools/replay.mjs --incident <INC-id> --core-dir core --evidence-dir packet/evidence
    reruns the window n-60..n+120 on core/ against the cached oracle frames; prints the first mismatch or "clean"
node tools/replay.mjs --family <family> --core-dir core --roms packet/roms.json
    scores one family; prints its reading as JSON
ROMs and oracle frames are reached through $RATCHET_ROMS and $RATCHET_CACHE.

## Skills
.agents/skills/ holds the skills shown to this attempt, read-only. Mark each one in RESULT.json.

## End by writing packet/RESULT.json
{ "dispositions": { "<SKL-id>": "applied" | "considered-not-applicable" },
  "off_map": null | "<one sentence naming a lesson you relied on that no shown skill holds>",
  "beliefs": [ { "claim": "<a hardware claim>", "false_if": "<the observation that falsifies it>" } ],
  "summary": "<one sentence: what the diff changes>" }

payload.prompt:
# Repair task

Edit files under core/ only. The gate reads only the diff of core/** and refuses a diff that touches any other
path, adds a literal over the gate's literal limit, or contains the incident's frame hash or trace bytes.
Your budget is 90 model steps and 1350 s of wall clock, after which you are stopped and an empty diff is refused, so make your first edit under core/ by step 45 (675 s) and refine it with the replay after.

## Core API (core/index.ts)
export function createCore(rom: Uint8Array): Core;  // step, runFrame, runToCounter(n), cpu, read, frame() (160*144 shades 0..3),
                                                    // serial, cycles, setButtons(mask), snapshot/restore, tap
export const HANDLERS: Record<HandlerId, string>;  // handler id -> implementing file under core/

## The task
packet/task.json names the task. For an incident: packet/incident.json (first diverging counter, signature),
packet/trace.json (inputs and the window n-60 .. n+120), and the evidence files (core.png, oracle.png, diff.png,
regwrites.jsonl, window.json) under packet/evidence/. packet/roms.json lists the ROMs per family.

## Replay
node tools/replay.mjs --incident <INC-id> --core-dir core --evidence-dir packet/evidence
    reruns the window n-60..n+120 on core/ against the cached oracle frames; prints the first mismatch or "clean"
node tools/replay.mjs --family <family> --core-dir core --roms packet/roms.json
    scores one family; prints its reading as JSON
ROMs and oracle frames are reached through $RATCHET_ROMS and $RATCHET_CACHE.

## Skills
.agents/skills/ holds the skills shown to this attempt, read-only. Mark each one in RESULT.json.

## End by writing packet/RESULT.json
{ "dispositions": { "<SKL-id>": "applied" | "considered-not-applicable" },
  "off_map": null | "<one sentence naming a lesson you relied on that no shown skill holds>",
  "beliefs": [ { "claim": "<a hardware claim>", "false_if": "<the observation that falsifies it>" } ],
  "summary": "<one sentence: what the diff changes>" }

# Repair task

Edit files under core/ only. The gate reads only the diff of core/** and refuses a diff that touches any other
path, adds a literal over the gate's literal limit, or contains the incident's frame hash or trace bytes.
Your budget is 90 model steps and 1350 s of wall clock, after which you are stopped and an empty diff is refused, so make your first edit under core/ by step 45 (675 s) and refine it with the replay after.

## Core API (core/index.ts)
export function createCore(rom: Uint8Array): Core;  // step, runFrame, runToCounter(n), cpu, read, frame() (160*144 shades 0..3),
                                                    // serial, cycles, setButtons(mask), snapshot/restore, tap
export const HANDLERS: Record<HandlerId, string>;  // handler id -> implementing file under core/

## The task
packet/task.json names the task. For an incident: packet/incident.json (first diverging counter, signature),
packet/trace.json (inputs and the window n-60 .. n+120), and the evidence files (core.png, oracle.png, diff.png,
regwrites.jsonl, window.json) under packet/evidence/. packet/roms.json lists the ROMs per family.

## Replay
node tools/replay.mjs --incident <INC-id> --core-dir core --evidence-dir packet/evidence
    reruns the window n-60..n+120 on core/ against the cached oracle frames; prints the first mismatch or "clean"
node tools/replay.mjs --family <family> --core-dir core --roms packet/roms.json
    scores one family; prints its reading as JSON
ROMs and oracle frames are reached through $RATCHET_ROMS and $RATCHET_CACHE.

## Skills
.agents/skills/ holds the skills shown to this attempt, read-only. Mark each one in RESULT.json.

## End by writing packet/RESULT.json
{ "dispositions": { "<SKL-id>": "applied" | "considered-not-applicable" },

24|; Window reactivation zero pixels should be present when window is already
25|; activated and the pixel that the window reactivates on is on the same 
26|; cycle as the window tile nametable read.

28|INCLUDE "inc/hardware.inc"
29|
30|
31|SECTION "wram", WRAM0
32|
33|counter::
34|    ds 1
35|
36|
37|SECTION "vblank", ROM0[$40]
38|

40|
41|
42|SECTION "lcdc", ROM0[$48]
43|
44|    jp lcdc_handler     
45|
46|

48|
49|    nop                                       
50|    jp main                          
51|
52|
53|SECTION "main", ROM0[$150]
54|
55|main::
56|
57|    di
58|    ld sp, $fffe
59|
60|    xor a
61|    ld [counter], a
62|
63|    call reset_registers
64|    call reset_oam
65|
66|    ; select mode 2 lcdc interrupt
67|    ld a, $20
68|    ldh [rSTAT], a
69|
70|    ; enable vblank and lcdc interrupts
71|    ld a, $03
72|    ldh [rIE], a
73|
74|    call copy_font
75|
76|    ; background is filled with 'B'
77|    ld a, $42
78|    call fill_vram_9800
79|
80|    ; window is filled with 'W'
81|    ld a, $57
82|    call fill_vram_9c00
83|
84|
85|    ; turn the screen on, $9C00-$9FFF window tile map, window on, bg tile data $8000-$8FFF, 
86|    ; bg tile map $9800-$9BFF, obj size 8*8, obj display on, bg display on
87|    ld a, $f3
88|    ldh [rLCDC], a
89|
90|    ld a, 4
91|    ldh [rWY], a
92|
93|    ld a, 80
94|    ldh [rWX], a 
95|
96|    ld a, $ff
97|    ldh [rOBP0], a
98|
99|    ld a, $e4
100|    ldh [rBGP], a
101|
102|    ; load c with address of WX register
103|    ld c, LOW(rWX)
104|
105|    ; enable interrupts
106|    ei
107|
108|

110|    REPT 1200
111|    nop
112|    ENDR
113|
114|    jp nop_slide
115|

117|
118|    ; let it run for 3 frames
119|    ld a, [counter]
120|    inc a
121|
122|    cp 3
123|    jp nz, .continue
124|
125|    ; source code breakpoint - good time to take a screenshot to compare
126|    ld b,b
127|
128|.continue:
129|
130|    ld [counter], a
131|    reti
132|
133|
134|lcdc_handler::
135|
136|    ; 20 cycles interrupt dispatch + 12 cycles to jump here: 32
137|
138|
139|    ; set WX: 16 cycles
140|    ld a, $05
141|    ld [c], a
142|
143|    ; read LY: 12 cycles
144|    ldh a, [rLY]
145|
146|    REPT 6
147|    nop
148|    ENDR    
149|
150|    ; set WX to value of LY: 8 cycles
151|    ld [c], a
152|
153|    REPT 20
154|    nop
155|    ENDR
156|
157|    ; position window in middle of the screen
158|    ld a, 80
159|    ld [c], a
160|
161|    ; reset the return address to the top of the nops loop
162|    pop hl
163|    ld hl, nop_slide
164|    push hl
165|
166|    reti
167|
168|
169|

  "output": "# The Comprehensive Game Boy PPU Documentation

These are my notes/findings based on the results of my test ROMs and subsequent implementation in my Game Boy emulator: [Beaten Dying Moon](https://mattcurrie.com/bdm-demo/)

Familiarity with Kevin Horton's [Nitty Gritty Gameboy Cycle Timing](http://blog.kevtris.org/blogfiles/Nitty%20Gritty%20Gameboy%20VRAM%20Timing.txt) is assumed.  

Any corrections or improvements are welcomed, especially for any already "known" information.

## Registers

### LCDC `$FF40`

#### TILE_SEL (bit 4)

The `TILE_SEL` bit of the `LCDC` register controls which area of VRAM is accessed when reading tile bitplane data.

| TILE_SEL | VRAM Range               |
| -------- | ------------------------ |
|        0 | $8800 - $97FF            |
|        1 | $8000 - $8FFF (OBJ area) |

The value of this bit can be written to at any time.

`TILE_SEL` is read during the `0` and `1` stages of background tile data fetching. Changing its value during background tile data fetch allows for mixing tile bitplane data from two different tile patterns.

On the CGB, there is strange behaviour if the value of this bit changes on particular T-cycles of the background tile data fetch. The following behaviour has been observed:

- On all CGB revisions, setting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as a bitplane data read will cause it to use either:
  - bitplane 1 data from the most recently drawn sprite as bitplane data, if any, or
  - bitplane 1 data from the most recently drawn tile as when `TILE_SEL` was last reset, if any, or
  - bitplane 0 or 1 data from the read in progress during pixel 159/160 (?) on the previous row when the tile fetcher is interrupted. The timing of which bitplane is selected differs between CGB revisions.
- On all CGB revisions, excluding CPU CGB D, resetting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as a bitplane data read will cause the **tile index** to be instead used as the data for that bitplane.
- On CPU CGB D, resetting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as the bitplane 1 data read will cause the PPU to instead read the bitplane data from the address for bitplane 0.

#### WIN_EN (bit 5)

If WIN_EN is set then the window will be displayed when the WX and WY conditions are satisifed.

Familiarity with Kevin Horton's [Nitty Gritty Gameboy Cycle Timing](http://blog.kevtris.org/blogfiles/Nitty%20Gritty%20Gameboy%20VRAM%20Timing.txt) is assumed.  

Any corrections or improvements are welcomed, especially for any already "known" information.

## Registers

### LCDC `$FF40`

#### TILE_SEL (bit 4)

The `TILE_SEL` bit of the `LCDC` register controls which area of VRAM is accessed when reading tile bitplane data.

| TILE_SEL | VRAM Range               |
| -------- | ------------------------ |
|        0 | $8800 - $97FF            |
|        1 | $8000 - $8FFF (OBJ area) |

The value of this bit can be written to at any time.

`TILE_SEL` is read during the `0` and `1` stages of background tile data fetching. Changing its value during background tile data fetch allows for mixing tile bitplane data from two different tile patterns.

On the CGB, there is strange behaviour if the value of this bit changes on particular T-cycles of the background tile data fetch. The following behaviour has been observed:

- On all CGB revisions, setting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as a bitplane data read will cause it to use either:
  - bitplane 1 data from the most recently drawn sprite as bitplane data, if any, or
  - bitplane 1 data from the most recently drawn tile as when `TILE_SEL` was last reset, if any, or
  - bitplane 0 or 1 data from the read in progress during pixel 159/160 (?) on the previous row when the tile fetcher is interrupted. The timing of which bitplane is selected differs between CGB revisions.
- On all CGB revisions, excluding CPU CGB D, resetting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as a bitplane data read will cause the **tile index** to be instead used as the data for that bitplane.
- On CPU CGB D, resetting `TILE_SEL` on the same T-cycle as the bitplane 1 data read will cause the PPU to instead read the bitplane data from the address for bitplane 0.

#### WIN_EN (bit 5)

If WIN_EN is set then the window will be displayed when the WX and WY conditions are satisifed.

Obscure behavior:

- WIN_EN can be disabled during mode 3.  The disabling will take effect at the end of the current window tile being drawn. When the current window tile has finished being drawn, the PPU will start drawing background tiles again.
- When the background resumes drawing it is on a tile boundary. The low 3 bits of SCX have no effect. 
- Setting WIN_EN again during mode 3 on the same scanline will have no effect unless WX has been updated to set the window to activate on a pixel that hasn't been drawn yet.
- If WX has been updated correctly and WIN_EN is set again then the PPU stops drawing the background, and will activate the window again, but it will start drawing the **next row** of the window, on the same scanline.

### SCY `$FF42`

The `SCY` register controls the Y scroll of the background tile map.  

The `SCY` register can be written to at any time. Writes will take effect immediately on the DMG. On CGB and AGB devices, writes appear to take effect 2 T-cycles later.

  "chunk_id": "exec-37-1",
  "command": "sed -n '290,520p' /tmp/fifo.txt",
  "description": "Read full Pixel FIFO doc text",
  "exit_code": 0,
  "terminal_status": "completed",
  "output": "Pixel FIFO

Introduction

FIFO stands for 
First In, First Out
. The first pixel to be pushed to the
FIFO is the first pixel to be popped off. In theory that sounds great,
in practice there are a lot of intricacies.

There are two pixel FIFOs. One for background pixels and one for object
(sprite) pixels. These two FIFOs are not shared. They are independent
of each other. The two FIFOs are mixed only when popping items. Objects
take priority unless they’re transparent (color 0) which will be
explained in detail later. Each FIFO can hold up to 16 pixels. The FIFO
and Pixel Fetcher work together to ensure that the FIFO always contains
at least 8 pixels at any given time, as 8 pixels are required for the
Pixel Rendering operation to take place. Each FIFO is manipulated only
during mode 3 (pixel transfer).

Each pixel in the FIFO has four properties:

Color: a value between 0 and 3

Palette: on CGB a value between 0 and 7 and on DMG this only applies to objects

Sprite Priority: on CGB this is the OAM index for the object and on DMG this doesn’t exist

Background Priority: holds the value of the 
OBJ-to-BG Priority
 bit

FIFO Pixel Fetcher

The fetcher fetches a row of 8 background or window pixels and queues
them up to be mixed with object pixels. The pixel fetcher has 5 steps.
The first four steps take 2 dots each and the fifth step is attempted
every dot until it succeeds. The order of the steps are as follows:

Get tile

Get tile data low

Get tile data high

Sleep

Push

Get Tile

This step determines which background/window tile to fetch pixels from.
By default the tilemap used is the one at $9800 but certain conditions
can change that.

When LCDC.3 is enabled and the X coordinate of the current scanline is
not inside the window then tilemap $9C00 is used.

When LCDC.6 is enabled and the X coordinate of the current scanline is
inside the window then tilemap $9C00 is used.

The fetcher keeps track of which X and Y coordinate of the tile it’s on:

If the current tile is a window tile, the X coordinate for the window
tile is used, otherwise the following formula is used to calculate
the X coordinate: ((SCX / 8) + fetcher’s X coordinate) & $1F. Because of
this formula, fetcherX can be between 0 and 31.

If the current tile is a window tile, the Y coordinate for the window
tile is used, otherwise the following formula is used to calculate
the Y coordinate: (currentScanline + SCY) & 255. Because of this formula,
fetcherY can be between 0 and 255.

The fetcher’s X and Y coordinate can then be used to get the tile from
VRAM. However, if the PPU’s access to VRAM is 
blocked

then the value for the tile is read as $FF.

CGB can access both tile index and the attributes in the same clock
dot.

Get Tile Data Low

Check LCDC.4 for which tilemap to use. At this step CGB also needs to
check which VRAM bank to use and check if the tile is flipped vertically.
Once the tilemap, VRAM and vertical flip is calculated the tile data
is retrieved from VRAM. However, if the PPU’s access to VRAM is

blocked
 then the tile data is read as $FF.

The tile data retrieved in this step will be used in the push steps.

Get Tile Data High

Same as Get Tile Data Low except the tile address is incremented by 1.

The tile data retrieved in this step will be used in the push steps.

This also pushes a row of background/window pixels to the FIFO. This
extra push is not part of the 8 steps, meaning there’s 3 total chances to
push pixels to the background FIFO every time the complete fetcher steps
are performed.

Push

Pushes a row of background/window pixels to the FIFO. Since tiles are 8
pixels wide, a “row” of pixels is 8 pixels from the tile to be rendered
based on the X and Y coordinates calculated in the previous steps.

Pixels are only pushed to the background FIFO if it’s empty.

This is where the tile data retrieved in the two Tile Data steps will
come in handy. Depending on if the tile is flipped horizontally the
pixels will be pushed to the background FIFO differently. If the tile
is flipped horizontally the pixels will be pushed LSB first. Otherwise
they will be pushed MSB first.

Sleep

Do nothing.

VRAM Access

At various times during PPU operation read access to VRAM is blocked and
the value read is $FF:

LCD turning off

At scanline 0 on CGB when not in double speed mode

When switching from mode 3 to mode 0

On CGB when searching OAM and index 37 is reached

At various times during PPU operation read access to VRAM is restored:

At scanline 0 on DMG and CGB when in double speed mode

On DMG when searching OAM and index 37 is reached

After switching from mode 2 (oam search) to mode 3 (pixel transfer)

NOTE: These conditions are checked only when entering STOP mode and the
PPU’s access to VRAM is always restored upon leaving STOP mode.

Mode 3 Operation

As stated before the pixel FIFO only operates during mode 3 (pixel
transfer). At the beginning of mode 3 both the background and OAM FIFOs
are cleared.

The Window

When rendering the window the background FIFO is cleared and the fetcher
is reset to step 1. When WX is 0 and the SCX & 7 > 0 mode 3 is shortened
by 1 dot.

When the window has already started rendering there is a bug that occurs
when WX is changed mid-scanline. When the value of WX changes after the
window has started rendering and the new value of WX is reached again,
a pixel with color value of 0 and the lowest priority is pushed onto the
background FIFO.

Sprites

The following is performed for each object on the current scanline if
LCDC.1 is enabled (this condition is ignored on CGB) and the X coordinate
of the current scanline has an object on it. If those conditions are not
met then object fetching is 
canceled
.

At this point the 
fetcher
 is advanced one step
until it’s at step 5 or until the background FIFO is not empty. Advancing
the fetcher one step here lengthens mode 3 by 1 dot. This process may
be 
canceled
 after the fetcher has advanced a
step.

When SCX & 7 > 0 and there is an object at X coordinate 0 of the current
scanline then mode 3 is lengthened. The amount of dots this lengthens
mode 3 by is whatever the lower 3 bits of SCX are. After this penalty is
applied object fetching may be canceled. Note that the timing of the
penalty is not confirmed. It may happen before or after waiting for the
fetcher. More research needs to be done.

After checking for objects at X coordinate 0 the fetcher is advanced two
steps. The first advancement lengthens mode 3 by 1 dot and the second
advancement lengthens mode 3 by 3 dots. After each fetcher advancement
there is a chance for an object fetch cancel to occur.

The lower address for the row of pixels of the target object tile is now
retrieved and lengthens mode 3 by 1 dot. Once the address is retrieved
this is the last chance for object fetch cancel to occur. Exiting
object fetch lengthens mode 3 by 1 dot. The upper address for the
target object tile is now retrieved and does not shorten mode 3.

At this point 
VRAM Access
 is checked for the lower and
upper addresses for the target object. Before any mixing is done, if the
OAM FIFO doesn’t have at least 8 pixels in it then transparent pixels
with the lowest priority are pushed onto the OAM FIFO. Once this is done
each pixel of the target object row is checked. On CGB, horizontal flip
is checked here. If the target object pixel is not white and the pixel in
the OAM FIFO 
is
 white, or if the pixel in the OAM FIFO has higher
priority than the target object’s pixel, then the pixel in the OAM FIFO
is replaced with the target object’s properties.

Now it’s time to 
render a pixel
! The same process
described in Object Fetch Canceling is performed: a pixel is rendered and
the fetcher is advanced one step. This advancement lengthens mode 3 by 1
dot if the X coordinate of the current scanline is not 160. If the X
coordinate is 160 the PPU stops processing objects (because they won’t be
visible).

Everything in this section is repeated for every object on the current
scanline unless it was decided that fetching should be canceled or the
X coordinate is 160.

Pixel Rendering

",
  "original_output_bytes": 8154,
  "original_output_tokens": 2039,
  "truncated": false
}

  "description": "Read rest of FIFO doc",
  "exit_code": 0,
  "terminal_status": "completed",
  "output": "
This is where the background FIFO and OAM FIFO are mixed. There are
conditions where either a background pixel or an object pixel will have
display priority.

If there are pixels in the background and OAM FIFOs then a pixel is
popped off each. If the OAM pixel is not transparent and LCDC.1 is
enabled then the OAM pixel’s background priority property is used if it’s
the same or higher priority as the background pixel’s background priority.

Pixels won’t be pushed to the LCD if there is nothing in the background
FIFO or the current pixel is pixel 160 or greater.

If LCDC.0 is disabled then the background is disabled on DMG and the
background pixel won’t have priority on CGB. When the background pixel
is disabled the pixel color value will be 0, otherwise the color value
will be whatever color pixel was popped off the background FIFO. When the
pixel popped off the background FIFO has a color value other than 0 and
it has priority then the object pixel will be discarded.

At this point, on DMG, the color of the pixel is retrieved from the BGP
register and pushed to the LCD. On CGB when 
palette access

is blocked a black pixel is pushed to the LCD.

When an object pixel has priority, the color value is retrieved from the
popped pixel from the OAM FIFO. On DMG the color for the pixel is
retrieved from either the OBP1 or OBP0 register depending on the pixel’s
palette property. If the palette property is 1 then OBP1 is used,
otherwise OBP0 is used. The pixel is then pushed to the LCD. On CGB when
palette access is blocked, a black pixel is pushed to the LCD.

The pixel is then finally pushed to the LCD.

CGB Palette Access

At various times during PPU operation read access to the CGB palette is
blocked and a black pixel pushed to the LCD when rendering pixels:

LCD turning off

First HBlank of the frame

When searching OAM and index 37 is reached

After switching from mode 2 (oam search) to mode 3 (pixel transfer)

When entering HBlank (mode 0) and not in double speed mode, blocked 2 dots later no matter what

At various times during PPU operation read access to the CGB palette is
restored and pixels are pushed to the LCD normally when rendering pixels:

At the end of mode 2 (oam search)

For only 2 dots when entering HBlank (mode 0) and in double speed mode

Note

These conditions are checked only when entering STOP mode and the
PPU’s access to CGB palettes is always restored upon leaving STOP mode.

Object fetching may be canceled if LCDC.1 is disabled while the PPU is
fetching an object from OAM. This canceling lengthens mode 3 by the amount
of dots the previous instruction took plus the residual dots left for
the PPU to process. When OAM fetching is canceled, a pixel is 
rendered
, and
the 
fetcher

lengthens mode 3 by 1 dot if the current pixel is not 160. If the
current pixel is 160 the PPU stops processing objects because they won’t
be visible.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 
 
 

 
 
 

 

 

 

",

Values in the range 0–255 may be used. The PPU calculates the bottom-right coordinates of the viewport with those formulas: `bottom := (SCY + 143) % 256` and `right := (SCX + 159) % 256`. As suggested by the modulo operations, in case the values are larger than 255 they will "wrap around" towards the top-left corner of the tilemap. ## Mid-frame behavior The scroll registers are re-read on each [tile fetch](<#Get Tile>), except for the low 3 bits of `SCX`, which are only read at the beginning of the scanline (for the initial shifting of pixels). All models before the CGB-D read the Y coordinate once for each bitplane (so a very precisely timed `SCY` write allows "desyncing" them), but CGB-D and later use the same Y coordinate for both no matter what. =========== LCDC: # LCD Control ## FF40 — LCDC: LCD control **LCDC** is the main **LCD C**ontrol register. Its bits toggle what elements are displayed on the screen, and how. {{#bits 8 > "" 7:"LCD & PPU enable" 6:"Window tile map" 5:"Window enable" 4:"BG & Window tiles" 3:"BG tile map" 2:"OBJ size" 1:"OBJ enable" 0:"BG & Window enable / priority"; }} - **[LCD & PPU enable](<#LCDC.7 — LCD enable>)**: `0` = Off; `1` = On - **[Window tile map area](<#LCDC.6 — Window tile map area>)**: `0` = 9800–9BFF; `1` = 9C00–9FFF - **[Window enable](<#LCDC.5 — Window enable>)**: `0` = Off; `1` = On - **[BG & Window tile data area](<#LCDC.4 — BG and Window tile data area>)**: `0` = 8800–97FF; `1` = 8000–8FFF - **[BG tile map area](<#LCDC.3 — BG tile map area>)**: `0` = 9800–9BFF; `1` = 9C00–9FFF - **[OBJ size](<#LCDC.2 — OBJ size>)**: `0` = 8×8; `1` = 8×16 - **[OBJ enable](<#LCDC.1 — OBJ enable>)**: `0` = Off; `1` = On - **[BG & Window enable / priority](<#LCDC.0 — BG and Window enable/priority>)** *\[Different meaning in CGB Mode\]*: `0` = Off; `1` = On ### LCDC.7 — LCD enable This bit controls whether the LCD is on and the PPU is active. Setting it to 0 turns both off, which grants immediate and full access to VRAM, OAM, etc. :::danger CAUTION Stopping LCD operation (Bit 7 from 1 to 0) may be performed during VBlank ONLY, disabling the display outside of the VBlank period may damage the hardware by burning in a black horizontal line similar to that which appears when the GB is turned off. This appears to be a serious issue. Nintendo is reported to reject any games not following this rule. ::: When the display is disabled the screen is blank, which on DMG is displayed as a white "whiter" than color \#0. On SGB, the screen doesn't turn white, it appears that the previous picture sticks to the screen. (TODO: research this more.) When re-enabling the LCD, the PPU will immediately start drawing again, but the screen will stay blank during the first frame. ### LCDC.6 — Window tile map area This bit controls which background map the Window uses for rendering. When it's clear (0), the \$9800 tilemap is used, otherwise it's the \$9C00 one. ### LCDC.5 — Window enable This bit controls whether the window shall be displayed or not. This bit is overridden on DMG by [bit 0](<#LCDC.0 — BG and Window enable/priority>) if that bit is clear. Changing the value of this register mid-frame triggers several more complex behaviours: [see the corresponding chapter](<#Window mid-frame behavior>). ### LCDC.4 — BG and Window tile data area This bit controls which [addressing mode](<#VRAM Tile Data>) the BG and Window use to pick tiles. Objects (sprites) aren't affected by this, and will always use the \$8000 addressing mode. ### LCDC.3 — BG tile map area This bit works similarly to [LCDC bit 6](<#LCDC.6 — Window tile map area>): if the bit is clear (0), the BG uses tilemap $9800, otherwise tilemap $9C00. ### LCDC.2 — OBJ size This bit controls the size of all objects (1 tile or 2 stacked vertically). Be cautious when changing object size mid-frame. Changing from 8×8 to 8×16 pixels mid-frame within 8 scanlines of the bottom of an object causes the object's second tile to be visible for the rest of those 8 lines. If the size is changed during mode 2 or 3, remnants of objects in range could "leak" into the other tile and cause artifacts. ### LCDC.1 — OBJ enable This bit toggles whether objects are displayed or not. This can be toggled mid-frame, for example to avoid objects being displayed on top of a status bar or text box. (Note: toggling mid-scanline might have funky results on DMG? Investigation needed.) ### LCDC.0 — BG and Window enable/priority LCDC.0 has different meanings depending on Game Boy type and Mode: #### Non-CGB Mode (DMG, SGB and CGB in compatibility mode): BG and Window display When Bit 0 is cleared, both background and window become blank (white), and the [Window Display Bit](<#LCDC.5 — Window enable>) is ignored in that case. Only objects may still be displayed (if enabled in Bit 1). #### CGB Mode: BG and Window master priority When Bit 0 is cleared, the background and window lose their priority - the objects will be always displayed on top of background and window, independently of the priority flags in OAM and BG Map attributes. When Bit 0 is set, pixel priority is resolved [as described here](<#BG-to-OBJ Priority in CGB Mode>). ## Using LCDC LCDC is a powerful tool: each bit controls a lot of behavior, and can be modified at any time during the frame. ", "original_output_bytes": 5884, "original_output_tokens": 1471, "truncated": false }
